questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
One of the main reasons I chose to study in London was the opportunity to experience education in a different academic setting than Denmark. London is home to some of the world's most respected universities, including Queen Mary University of London, where I studied. The university’s strong reputation, combined with its diverse range of courses, made it an attractive choice.

I was particularly interested in studying my courses from a British perspective, as this allowed me to gain new insights into political science, especially regarding European politics and the UK's relationship with the EU. Additionally, Queen Mary offered elective courses that I would not have had the opportunity to take at the University of Copenhagen, allowing me to broaden my academic horizon.

Beyond academics, London itself was a key factor in my decision. As a global city with a rich history and vibrant cultural life, it provided a unique and inspiring environment to live and study in. Lastly, having an exchange semester at a well-known London university is also a valuable addition to my resume, as it demonstrates adaptability, international experience, and academic engagement in a different setting.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I had a great experience studying abroad. It was exciting to live in London, explore a new environment, and meet people from different backgrounds. The city itself offers endless opportunities, both academically and socially, making it a fantastic place to study.

One of the highlights of my time at Queen Mary University of London was the opportunity to join university sports teams, which added a great social and physical aspect to my exchange experience.

Academically, the courses were interesting, and the teaching style provided a different perspective compared to my home university. However, I found that the academic level, while high, was not as challenging as at the University of Copenhagen. As a result, some aspects of my courses were less challenging than expected. Nonetheless, studying in London was an incredibly rewarding experience, and I would highly recommend it to others.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Overall, it was fairly easy to find the necessary information upon arrival. However, I found that Queen Mary’s website, particularly regarding course details, was not always as comprehensive or informative as I had hoped. Some aspects of course selection and academic expectations could have been explained more clearly, which would have made the transition smoother.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Upon arrival at the university, we had a welcome day where we received important information about various aspects of student life. This included practical guidance on living on campus, using the library, connecting with other students, joining sports clubs, accessing IT services, and getting involved in student organizations.

We were also given details about our exams and how to contact professors, which was helpful in understanding the academic structure at Queen Mary. The welcome session provided a good introduction to university life.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
While Queen Mary University of London provided a well-structured general orientation covering student life, campus resources, and administrative procedures, I was extremely dissatisfied with the handling of academic matters, particularly course selection and availability.

Before my arrival, I had engaged in extensive communication with both Queen Mary and the University of Copenhagen, to ensure that my courses were properly pre-approved. A key reason for choosing Queen Mary was the opportunity to take The UK and the EU, which was essential for fulfilling my academic requirements. I had gone through a rigorous process of gathering course descriptions, securing approval from my home university, and confirming my eligibility to enroll. At no point during this process was I informed that the course would not be running in the fall semester.

Upon arriving in London, I was unexpectedly informed that The UK and the EU had been cancelled for the semester, despite it still being listed on Queen Mary’s website as available. This immediately put me in a difficult position, as there were no equivalent EU-related courses offered that could be transferred for credit. Had I been made aware of this beforehand, I could have planned accordingly and taken European Politics at my home university instead of being forced to scramble for a solution after my exchange had already begun.

Attempts to find an alternative course were met with slow responses and a lack of viable options. Queen Mary’s academic office was unable to offer any real assistance beyond suggesting unrelated courses, which were not applicable to my degree requirements. Their response largely placed the responsibility on me to resolve the situation, despite the fact that this issue arose due to their own administrative shortcomings.

After extensive back-and-forth communication between Queen Mary, my home university, and multiple faculty members, it became clear that there was no suitable replacement course available. As a result, I was ultimately forced to take European Politics remotely and sit for the exam at the University of Copenhagen upon my return. This situation was entirely avoidable and created unnecessary stress, logistical complications, and additional academic pressure during my exchange semester.

Overall, my experience with Queen Mary’s academic support was highly disappointing. The lack of transparency, poor communication, and inflexible course enrollment process made what should have been a straightforward study abroad experience unnecessarily difficult. Given these challenges, I cannot recommend that political science students apply for an exchange at Queen Mary in their fifth semester, as the uncertainty surrounding course availability poses a serious risk to academic progression.

While the university offered good general support for non-academic matters, the way this issue was handled left a lasting negative impression and significantly impacted my exchange experience.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Finding housing in London as a student can initially feel overwhelming, especially when trying to find something budget-friendly. The rental market moves incredibly fast, and many options are either extremely expensive or require long-term commitments that don’t align with an exchange semester.

At one point, I was close to accepting a small one-bedroom apartment for £1,400 per month, but I ultimately chose to stay at Dansk KFUK, a youth hostel/college-style accommodation. Although it meant sharing a room with three others, I ended up being very happy with my decision. The rent was only £400 per month, which included breakfast (and the option to get dinner), and the location in Hampstead was fantastic—an upscale, safe area with easy access to central London.

For those considering Dansk KFUK, they also offer a few single rooms and some student apartments in the area, so it's worth reaching out to check availability. Applications usually open in May, and I highly recommend applying early if you're interested.

In terms of studying while sharing a room, I found it manageable as long as I communicated with my roommates about when I needed quiet time. Additionally, the residence has common areas and a TV lounge, which are usually quiet and great for studying.

Beyond affordability, one of the biggest advantages of staying at a place like Dansk KFUK is the built-in social network. Many of the other residents were also exchange students or interns, including several political science and economics students. This made it easy to make friends and have a group to explore London with outside of university. The residence also organized occasional social events, which helped create a strong sense of community.

Overall, while finding housing in London can be challenging, I highly recommend considering alternative student accommodations like Dansk KFUK, especially if budget is a priority. It provides both affordability and a great social experience, making it a solid option for exchange students.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
The biggest thing to consider when living off campus in London is your budget. Rent is expensive, and everyday expenses such as transport, food, and going out can quickly add up.

Public transport, especially the Tube, is costly, so I highly recommend getting an Oyster card for zones 1 & 2 as soon as you arrive. It works similarly to a travel card and allows you to top up as needed, saving you a significant amount over time.

Another tip—bring a book. You’ll spend a lot of time on the Tube, and since mobile coverage isn’t available everywhere underground, having something to read makes the commutes much more enjoyable.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process at Queen Mary University of London was relatively straightforward in the beginning. I was contacted in May and asked to confirm my enrollment, which was easy to complete. Once I was officially in their system, I started receiving regular updates specifically for associate (exchange) students, which helped guide the next steps.

In June, Queen Mary opened pre-registration for course selection, allowing exchange students to indicate their preferred modules. However, final course confirmation only happened in September, when we had to re-confirm our choices and make any necessary adjustments.

Overall, the initial setup was smooth, but the two-step course registration process required some patience, as module availability wasn’t always guaranteed.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
Queen Mary University had a dedicated Global Opportunities Office with a team of around ten staff members responsible for assisting exchange students before, during, and after their time abroad.

In general, they were quite responsive, and it was relatively easy to get help when needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
The course registration process at Queen Mary University of London turned out to be more complicated than expected. While I was able to register for some of my preferred electives, the overall experience was frustrating due to a lack of transparency regarding course availability.

One major challenge was that even after pre-registering in June, there was no guarantee that courses would actually be available in September when final registration took place. This created a lot of uncertainty, as students had to wait until the semester started to confirm their schedules. The process was also highly competitive, with some courses filling up quickly and limited flexibility in swapping modules.

Communication from the university was inconsistent, making it difficult to get clear answers about which courses would run. Even though I had gone through the proper channels to secure my choices, I ultimately had to make unexpected adjustments that affected my academic plans.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: For future students, I would recommend having backup options for all courses and double-checking availability directly with both Queen Mary and the University of Copenhagen well in advance to avoid last-minute issues.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Queen Mary University of London has a dedicated School of Politics & International Relations, which offers a wide selection of courses. The variety of modules available was quite extensive, covering a broad range of topics within political science and international relations. Many of these courses were engaging and provided interesting perspectives, which I appreciated.

In terms of course availability, the selection was satisfactory, and there were plenty of options to explore different areas of study. However, students should be aware that while the range of courses looks promising on paper, actual course availability can be uncertain, as not all modules listed in advance will necessarily be offered in a given semester.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The academic level at Queen Mary University of London was generally lower than what I am used to at the University of Copenhagen. While the courses were interesting and covered relevant topics, they were often less demanding in terms of workload, critical engagement, and depth of analysis compared to similar courses at KU.

Assignments tended to be more structured, with clear guidelines that left less room for independent analytical thinking. The expectations for student performance also seemed lower, with fewer required readings and a more guided approach to coursework. While this made the semester more manageable, it also meant that some courses felt less academically challenging.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching style at Queen Mary University of London was very similar to that of the bachelor's program in Political Science at the University of Copenhagen. Each course typically consisted of one lecture per week, followed by a smaller seminar-style class (which they refer to as "seminars").

One key difference was the strict attendance policy for seminars. Attendance was mandatory, and absences were recorded, whereas at UCPH, participation is more flexible and your own responsible. However, class participation did not contribute to final grades, so while students were expected to attend, there was no formal assessment of engagement in discussions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend British Politics (POL243A) to future exchange students, especially given the current political landscape in the UK.

The course provides a solid intermediate-level grounding in contemporary British politics and government, covering key topics such as the UK’s political constitution, sovereign parliament, electoral politics, and cabinet government. Given the political developments in recent years—including Brexit, shifts in party dynamics, and ongoing constitutional debates—studying British politics from within the country added a unique and highly relevant perspective.

Additionally, the course is 100% coursework-based, which can be beneficial for those who prefer  assessments over high-stakes final exams. The combination of theoretical knowledge and practical political analysis makes this a highly engaging and valuable course for anyone interested in UK and comparative politics.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: One of the biggest unexpected costs was transport. While I knew London’s public transport was expensive, the daily expenses of using the Tube and buses added up quickly, even with an Oyster card. Additionally, some student discounts were not as significant as I had expected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transport and eating out.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Queen Mary University of London offered a wide range of clubs and societies, covering everything from sports and cultural groups to academic and special interest societies. Early in the semester, the university hosted a Welcome Fair, where students had the opportunity to explore different clubs, meet members, and sign up for activities or trials for sports teams.

I personally had a great experience playing football at the university, which became a major part of my exchange. Queen Mary has five football teams, and through training sessions and matches, I built strong friendships with teammates. The football club became my main social circle, and I spent several hours each week both on and off the field with them.

For students looking to get involved socially and stay active, the variety of sports clubs, student societies, and social events at Queen Mary makes it easy to find a community and connect with others.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend joining a sports club. Whether or not you play at a high level, getting involved in university sports is a great way to meet people, stay active, and have a structured social outlet throughout the semester. The football club was an incredible experience for me, but there are many other sports available for students at different skill levels.

Another recommendation is to join a cultural or nationality-based society. I was a member of the Queen Mary Scandinavian Society, which was a fantastic way to meet other Nordic students and build friendships with people who had similar backgrounds and experiences. These societies often host social gatherings, events, and networking opportunities, making them a great way to feel at home while studying abroad.

For any exchange student, getting involved in both a sports club and a social society can make a huge difference in building friendships and making the most of the experienc

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
There’s no shortage of things to do in and around London, but I highly recommend a mix of classic British experiences, exploring the city’s green spaces, and taking short trips outside of London.

First and foremost, going to pubs is a must. London has a fantastic pub culture, and spending an afternoon or evening in a traditional pub is one of the best ways to experience local life, whether it’s for a Guinness, a Sunday roast, or even a pub quiz night.

Another great way to spend weekends is by visiting the many parks across the city. Hyde Park, Regent’s Park, and Hampstead Heath are perfect for running.  London’s parks offer a great escape and are worth exploring in different seasons.

For longer weekends or holidays, I strongly recommend taking day trips to other major British cities. Oxford and Cambridge are both stunning university towns with a lot of history and charm, while Brighton offers a great coastal escape. Manchester, Liverpool, and Edinburgh are also fantastic destinations if you want to experience different parts of the UK.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The best way to socialize with local students is to join a sports club or student society. Sports teams, in particular, offer a great way to meet people, as training and matches create a strong sense of community. Additionally, going to pubs, attending university events, and engaging in group activities through clubs or societies make it easier to connect with both local and international students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn’t experience any significant cultural differences that were particularly challenging.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
One of the things I appreciated most about British culture was the football culture. Football is a huge part of everyday life—everyone talks about it constantly, whether it’s Premier League matches, local teams, or just casual debates about the latest results.

Going to football matches at stadiums was an incredible experience. The atmosphere, the passion of the fans, and the sense of community around the sport made it unforgettable. Whether you're a big football fan or just interested in experiencing a key part of British culture, attending a match in London is something I highly recommend.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be prepared for course registration challenges – Some courses may not be available even if they were listed beforehand, so have backup options and confirm availability as early as possible.

Budget carefully – Rent, transport, and everyday expenses in London add up quickly. Get an Oyster card for zones 1 & 2 early on and be mindful of housing costs.

Join a sports club or society – It’s the best way to meet people and build a social circle. Football was a great experience for me, but there are many clubs to choose from.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not besides all the information, tips, and advice I've given on previous questions

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was truly immersing myself in British culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not really any.
